alalal-e85947-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 4: what an article of faith is by definition.

alalal-e85947-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's text asking whether Peter had faith in the passion.

alalal-e85947-d1e127.summary: Announces a major treatment of the articles of faith in five problems: what an article is by definition; what it is in reality; the number of articles in each creed; the differences between the creeds; and whether we must believe things that are not articles and how they relate to the articles.

alalal-e85947-d1e161.summary: Gives Richard of Saint Victor's definition: an article is an indivisible truth about God that constrains us to believe.

alalal-e85947-d1e177.summary: Gives the definition attributed to Isidore: an article is a perception of divine truth tending toward it.

alalal-e85947-d1e193.summary: Notes a definition some masters attribute to Hugh, 'an article is nature with grace', which is not found in his book as proposed.

alalal-e85947-d1e207.summary: First objection to Richard: 'indivisible' means where the creed's division stops, but creeds divide differently, so an article is not simply indivisible.

alalal-e85947-d1e231.summary: Second objection: an article is a joint of limb with limb, so it names where credibles are joined, not what they are resolved into by division.

alalal-e85947-d1e244.summary: Third objection: Augustine says the following limb has its power of motion in the joint; since motion toward the credible comes from the habit, faith by which we believe should rather be the article.

alalal-e85947-d1e261.summary: Fourth objection: not every article is about God, such as the resurrection of the flesh or the holy catholic Church.

alalal-e85947-d1e277.summary: Fifth objection: if 'constraining' means natural inclination, as a virtue is bound to its act and object, it belongs to faith by which one believes rather than what is believed.

alalal-e85947-d1e293.summary: Sixth objection: if it means constraint by evident truth convincing the intellect, it is false, since the chief articles are against the principles of reason and seem rather to deter from belief.

alalal-e85947-d1e309.summary: Introduces similar objections to Isidore's definition.

alalal-e85947-d1e316.summary: First objection: an article is not perception of truth but of the shadow and mirror of truth.

alalal-e85947-d1e325.summary: Further: some philosophers had a perception of truth tending to it, so they would have had articles.

alalal-e85947-d1e337.summary: Second objection: if 'tending' means by love, then someone in mortal sin who believes all articles with unformed faith would lack faith, which is false.

alalal-e85947-d1e350.summary: Declines to object to the definition attributed to Hugh, since its words are invented and falsely ascribed to him, as will be shown from his own words.

alalal-e85947-d1e361.summary: Solution: Richard defines what is believed, the articles, by form, proper matter and act. The generic form is truth, its contracting difference indivisibility; the matter is 'about God', since without indivisible truth about God there is no article, as the common definition shows: believing is assenting to first truth for its own sake and above all. Only divine truth is assented to absolutely for its own sake, 'for its own sake' naming efficient, final and formal cause: we believe by its causality, not our reasoning; for it, as nothing is greater; and through it alone, since first truth, unlike metaphysical principles true by divine light, is made true by nothing else. 'Constraining us to believe' names the efficient aspect.
claims: An article of faith is an indivisible truth about God that constrains belief, as Richard defines it.
Only divine truth is believed for its own sake as efficient, final and formal cause of assent.
concepts: first truth as cause of assent

alalal-e85947-d1e424.summary: Isidore's definition touches form and act, but not the proper meaning of the name, omitting what 'article' signifies, constraining and indivisibility.

alalal-e85947-d1e444.summary: Reply to the first objection: division is by the act of the divider or by the divisibility of the thing. In the Apostles' Creed articles are multiplied by the divider's act, so some remain undivided that could be divided by nature; the definition applies across creeds, with 'indivisible' sometimes negating only the act of division and sometimes also the potency, as will be explained in treating the creeds' differences.

alalal-e85947-d1e479.summary: Reply to the second: 'article' is taken materially as a joined member and formally as the joining of members; Richard takes it in the first sense, relative to the parts, while the second applies to the creed as a whole, which is the joining of material articles.

alalal-e85947-d1e509.summary: Reply to the third: faith's motion begins from the truth of the article, not the habit; the article's truth produces the habit by its likeness in the soul and makes it tend to that truth, so the motion begins from divine truth and returns through the article to it, a circle of the ray going out from eternity into the just soul and back, as Dionysius describes the procession of lights from the Father and their return to his unity.
claims: The truth of the article, not the habit, initiates the motion of faith, forming the habit by its likeness.

alalal-e85947-d1e556.summary: Reply to the fourth: every article is about God, since we believe the future resurrection only by divine truth and command (Damascene), and the Church's unity, forgiveness, baptism and sacraments avail only by divine truth working through the Holy Spirit; all are easily reduced to divine truth.
claims: Every article concerns God, since each depends on divine truth and action.

alalal-e85947-d1e585.summary: Reply to the fifth: the constraint is through a simple light from which the habit's light proceeds, so the article's truth, prior by nature, constrains.

alalal-e85947-d1e598.summary: Reply to the sixth: the argument would hold if the constraint were by complex reasoning, but it is rather like nature, convincing the intellect by the power of the simple light given, so that it tends to what it believes.

alalal-e85947-d1e616.summary: Reply on the philosophers: they had perception of divine truth only materially; it was human, through natural reasons, tending to truth by consent from reason, not in the manner of nature consonant with reason.
claims: Philosophers knew divine truths only materially, by reason, not by faith.

alalal-e85947-d1e636.summary: Reply on the false Christian: as said before, unformed faith of itself tends, but its subject does not follow.

alalal-e85947-d1e648.summary: On Hugh: his actual words, in part ten of De sacramentis, are that faith has two objects, creator and saviour; the first part concerns the works of creation in six days and the debt of nature, the second the works of restoration in six ages and the debt of grace. He means that some articles express the work of nature and some the work of grace, and does not intend to define an article.
claims: Hugh divides the articles into those of creation and those of restoration, without defining 'article'.

alalal-e85947.summary: Article 4 opens a five-part treatment of the articles of faith (their definition, reality, number, the differences of the creeds, and non-article beliefs) by asking what an article is by definition. Albert adopts Richard of Saint Victor's definition: an indivisible truth about God that constrains us to believe. Truth is its form, indivisibility its difference, God its matter, and constraint its act, since only divine truth is assented to for its own sake as efficient, final and formal cause. Isidore's definition gives form and act but misses what the name signifies, and the definition ascribed to Hugh is spurious: Hugh only divides the articles into those of creation and those of restoration. Albert explains that indivisibility can refer to the divider's act or to the thing's nature, and that an article is a joined member, the creed being their joining. The motion of faith begins from the article's truth, which forms the habit by its likeness and draws it back to God. Every article, even the resurrection and the Church, reduces to divine truth. The philosophers knew divine truths only materially, through reason.
claims: An article of faith is an indivisible truth about God that constrains us to believe.
Divine truth is the efficient, final and formal cause of the assent of faith.
Every article concerns God, since each depends on divine truth and action.
The truth of the article forms the habit of faith and initiates its motion back to God.
